Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A gray tabby cat asleep, curled on a folded mustard-yellow knitted blanket on a wooden sill

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

13 stepsFocal point: the cat's sleeping face and white paws Light: soft daylight from the window at the upper leftHow this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Blend the blue wallFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch flat: Block in the windowFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: Light the knit stitchesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: Block in the catFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch filbert: Paint the pale chest, muzzle, and pawsFilbert: flat with a rounded end, for soft-edged shapes
  • #4 round: Paint the pink ears and noseRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/4 inch angle: Paint the tabby stripesAngle: flat cut on a slant, for crisp corners and curves
  • small fan: Flick in the light furFan: bristles spread like a fan, for grass, fur, and soft blending

Also

  • White canvas or canvas board
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

Before you start

Mark halves and quarters on tape

Run a strip of masking tape along the top edge of the canvas and one down a side, and mark the middle and the quarters on each. Every step's Where picture has the same lines, so you can find its place on your canvas. (Chalk lines on the canvas would be painted over by the first coat; the tape stays.)

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on the same quarter grid as your tape: 1 The window; 2 The knitted blanket; 3 The sleeping cat. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, using the tape marks to place it.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • Side-to-side blend, first in step 1.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 3.
  • Dry brush, first in step 4. Try it on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 7.
  • Press and lift, first in step 8. Try a row of them on scrap paper first.
  • Thick to thin, first in step 12.
  • Flicking, first in step 13.

The basics

Before you start not checked yet

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.
Keep your colors clean not checked yet

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.
Colors dry darker not checked yet

Colors dry darker

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic looks lighter when wet than when dry.
  • Before a big area, paint a test swatch and let it dry before judging the mix.
Fixing a mistake not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.
Keep paint from drying on the palette not checked yet

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.
Let each layer dry not checked yet

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Light colors over dark need more than one coat not checked yet

Light colors over dark need more than one coat

Not checked yet

  • One coat of white or a light color over a dark one usually looks gray and patchy.
  • Expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry. Use the paint thick, with little water.
Making a color lighter or darker not checked yet

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
One light direction not checked yet

One light direction

Not checked yet

  • Pick where the light comes from and put every highlight on that side.
  • Each thing is built the same way: the whole shape in a darker or middle value, a lighter value on the side facing the light, then the lightest on a small area at the very edge. Each covers less than the one before.
The ugly stage not checked yet

The ugly stage

Not checked yet

  • Partway through, every painting looks flat or wrong. That's normal. Keep building.
  • Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
  • Details come last, and only on shapes that are already right.
How much water not checked yet

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.

The wall and the sill 2 steps

STEP 1 OF 13 · The wall and the sill, 1 of 2

Blend the blue wall

  1. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  2. Paints: Soft wall blue for the whole wall, and Warm taupe only below the window at the lower left.
  3. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: An even coat, neither thick nor thin.
  4. Start with the blue and stroke side to side across the whole wall. Without rinsing, pick up the taupe and paint it below the window at the lower left. Then stroke back over the join several times.
  5. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  6. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  7. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.

Tip: The light comes from the window at the upper left; every highlight in this painting sits on that side. Paint the blue straight across everything, right through where the cat and blanket will go, and add a little more blue to the mix for the narrow dark strip beside the window at the top.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. An even coat, neither thick nor thin.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 13 · The wall and the sill, 2 of 2

Blend the wooden sill

  1. Let the blue wall dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is a little above the 3/4 mark on the side tape.
  4. Paints, top to bottom: Sunlit peach, then Wood brown.
  5. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: An even coat, neither thick nor thin.
  6. Start with the sunlit peach at the left, and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the wood brown and paint it to the right and below. Then stroke back over the join several times.
  7. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  8. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  9. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.
  10. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Keep the sunlit peach at the left, under the window, and let the wood brown take over toward the right and the bottom edge. Run it straight under where the blanket will sit; the blanket covers it later.

The window 3 steps

STEP 3 OF 13 · The window, 1 of 3

Block in the window

  1. Let the wall and the sill dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge.
  4. Paint: Window gray-blue.
  5. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  6. Start with one simple shape: a tall rectangle for the whole window. Then add the rest in straight pieces: the ledge at its bottom and the strip down its right side.
  7. It should leave one flat gray-blue window shape made of a few pieces, with small overlaps between them.

Tip: The window is a tall rectangle at the left edge, from the top down to a little below the middle, as the Where picture shows.

Stroke: Building from pieces how to do it, not checked yet

Building from pieces

Not checked yet

Motion. Start with one simple shape (an oval, a circle, or a rectangle). Then add the rest in curved pieces on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges.

What it leaves. A shape made of distinct curved segments with small gaps or overlaps between them.

Then. Soften where the pieces meet only if the picture shows smooth ribs; otherwise leave the segments visible.

STEP 4 OF 13 · The window, 2 of 3

Light the window with leaves

  1. Let the window, and the wall and the sill dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is a little below the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge.
  3. Paint: Sage green.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: A dry brush, no water. Load only the tip, then wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  5. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  6. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  7. Leave what step 3 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.

Tip: Keep the leaves to the left strip of glass, between the frame bars. Let some gray-blue show between the marks, like sky through leaves.

Dry brush

Not checked yet

With. flat; old stiff flat (catches the canvas weave best)

Load. A dry brush, no water. Load only the tip, then wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel. It should feel dry and hard to apply.

Motion. Light pressure, skimming the surface.

What it leaves. Feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.

Then. Build up in several light passes.

Good for. cloud highlights, grass, wood and fences, highlights on round things

Skim, with almost no paint

STEP 5 OF 13 · The window, 3 of 3

Light the window frame bars

  1. Let the window, and the wall and the sill dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge.
  4. Paint: Warm white.
  5. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  6. Start with one simple shape: the tall upright bar. Then add the rest in pieces joined to it: the cross bar near the top and the ledge at the bottom.
  7. It should leave white bars made of distinct straight pieces, with small overlaps where they join.
  8. Leave what steps 3 and 4 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Paint the tall upright bar first, then the cross bar near the top and the ledge at the bottom joined to it. Leave a thin line of gray-blue along the right side of each bar as its shadow, and leave the leaves and the gray-blue glass showing at the far left.

The knitted blanket 3 steps

STEP 6 OF 13 · The knitted blanket, 1 of 3

Block in the blanket's two rolls

  1. Let the wall and the sill dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is at the bottom edge, and its right side is at the right edge.
  4. Paint: Deep ochre.
  5. Brush: 1 inch flat.
  6. Start with one simple shape: a long flat oval for the top roll. Then add the lower roll as a curved piece under it, like a ( turned on its side.
  7. It should leave two rolls made of distinct curved pieces, with a small gap or overlap where they meet.

Tip: The blanket is two long rolls stacked: a top roll the cat lies on, and a lower roll in front that reaches almost to the bottom edge. Paint over the bottom of where the cat will go.

STEP 7 OF 13 · The knitted blanket, 2 of 3

Shade the blanket's folds

  1. Let the knitted blanket, and the wall and the sill dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is at the bottom edge, and its right side is at the right edge.
  3. Paint: Ochre brown.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  5. Bend every stroke with the shape: along the curve of each roll, on its lower side and in the crease between them.
  6. It should leave marks that bend with the rolls, which is what makes them look round and thick.
  7. Leave what step 6 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.

Tip: The ochre brown is one thin crease line between the two rolls, running from the front left toward the middle as the Where picture shows. Keep it thin and broken; the rest of the blanket stays deep ochre.

STEP 8 OF 13 · The knitted blanket, 3 of 3

Light the knit stitches

  1. Let the knitted blanket, and the wall and the sill dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is at the bottom edge, and its right side is at the right edge.
  3. Paint: Mustard yellow.
  4. Brush: #8 round. Load: Paint loaded well into the belly of the brush, creamy, not runny.
  5. Touch down with the tip, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so the stroke ends on the tip.
  6. It should leave a teardrop or comma shape, wide where you pressed and pointed where you lifted; two leaning together make one stitch.
  7. Leave what steps 6 and 7 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: A blob instead of a teardrop. Too much paint, or too slow a lift. Fix: use less paint and lift faster.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Each stitch is two commas leaning together into a small V, in rows that run along each roll. Leave the deep ochre showing between the stitches; that's what makes the knit look thick.

The cat's shape 3 steps

STEP 9 OF 13 · The cat's shape, 1 of 3

Block in the cat

  1. Let the knitted blanket and the window dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  4. Inside the outlined area. Its top is a little below the top edge, and its right side is at the right edge.
  5. Paint: Cat gray.
  6. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  7. Start with one simple shape: a big oval for the body. Then add the rest in curved pieces: a circle for the head on its upper left, two triangle ears, and the curled back leg along the bottom.
  8. It should leave one gray cat shape made of distinct curved pieces, with small overlaps where they meet.

Tip: The body is one big oval lying on the blanket, filling most of the canvas to the right. The head is a circle on its upper left, tilted down onto the paws, with two triangle ears: one pointing up, one pointing left toward the window. Keep the gray off the window's white cross bar at the top left, even where the picture shows a gray patch on it.

Technique: A furry animal with markings Technique not checked yet

STEP 10 OF 13 · The cat's shape, 2 of 3

Paint the pale chest, muzzle, and paws

  1. Let the sleeping cat and the knitted blanket dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is a little below the top edge, and its left side is a little right of the left edge.
  3. Paint: Pale fur.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch filbert.
  5. Bend every stroke with the shape: around each paw, and along the way the fur lies on the chest and muzzle.
  6. It should leave marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes it look round or sloped.
  7. Leave what step 9 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Pale fur is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.

Tip: The white is the muzzle under the eyes, a patch on the chest below and to the right of the face, and two round front paws resting on the blanket. Paint the paws as two plump ovals, then a few pale strokes inside each ear. Finish with a few whiskers: thin pale lines pulled out from the muzzle with the very edge of the brush.

STEP 11 OF 13 · The cat's shape, 3 of 3

Paint the pink ears and nose

  1. Let the sleeping cat and the window dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is a little below the top edge, and its right side is at the right edge.
  3. Paint: Soft pink.
  4. Brush: #4 round. Load: Paint loaded well into the belly of the brush, creamy, not runny.
  5. Touch down with the tip, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so the stroke ends on the tip.
  6. It should leave a teardrop or comma shape inside each ear, wide at the base and pointed toward the tip.
  7. Leave what steps 9 and 10 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: A blob instead of a teardrop. Too much paint, or too slow a lift. Fix: use less paint and lift faster.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: One comma inside each ear, pointing to the ear's tip, leaving a gray rim around it. The nose is one tiny triangle where the white muzzle meets, just above the paws.

The cat's stripes and fur 2 steps

STEP 12 OF 13 · The cat's stripes and fur, 1 of 2

Paint the tabby stripes

  1. Let the cat's shape and the knitted blanket dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is a little below the top edge, and its right side is at the right edge.
  3. Paint: Charcoal gray.
  4. Brush: 1/4 inch angle.
  5. Press the full width of the brush for the thick part, then turn onto its edge or tip and lighten the pressure. With an angle brush, the lighter you press, the thinner the line.
  6. It should leave stripes that start wide and taper to a point.
  7. Leave what steps 9, 10 and 11 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.

Tip: The stripes curve around the body like bands on a barrel, wide at the back and tapering down toward the belly, and run up from the eyes toward the ears on the head. The darker shadow along the cat's back and belly goes in with this paint too. Last, the two closed eyes: short curved lines with the brush's tip, like smiles turned down.

STEP 13 OF 13 · The cat's stripes and fur, 2 of 2

Flick in the light fur

  1. Let the sleeping cat and the cat's shape dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is a little below the top edge, and its right side is at the right edge.
  3. Paint: Light fur gray.
  4. Brush: small fan. Load: Light paint. Too much makes flat blobs.
  5. A quick stroke from inside the fur outward in the direction the fur lies, lifting off as it goes, so each mark thins at the end.
  6. It should leave short tapered flicks of fur with broken tips.
  7. Leave what steps 9, 10, 11 and 12 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: The fur turns into a flat, smooth patch, or the stripes lose their edges. Too much paint on the brush, or the flicks are blended together.
  9. Fix: wipe the brush nearly dry, make each flick short and separate, and let it dry before adding more.
  10. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Flick along the body's curve, out from the face and back along the body, never across it. Put most flicks on the top and the window side, and let some cross the stripes' edges so they look soft.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A gray tabby cat asleep curled on a folded mustard-yellow knitted blanket on a wooden sill, a pale blue wall behind and a bright window at the top left.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: The image is a painting edge to edge with no bars, borders, captions, or watermark.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: none besides the subject (the window's leaves are a loose green blur). Textures of hundreds of items: the knit has roughly 60 to 80 visible stitches in rows, which one repeated mark (a pair of short curved dashes, a V) makes; the fur stripes are about 20 broad bands. Detail inside big shapes: whiskers and a few face lines, all small liner work. Parts: about 7, under the budget of 8.

Changed: nothing dropped or merged

Why: The source is already a loose painting with broad shapes; every texture is one repeated mark a beginner can make, so a beginner version would only cost money and blur the cat's face.

A gray tabby asleep on a mustard knitted blanket by a window. What matters is the cat's soft round shape, the white muzzle and paws, the curving stripes, and the warm yellow against the cool blue wall. The hard parts for a beginner are the curled body's proportions and making fur and knit from repeated marks, so the lesson builds the cat from simple pieces and the knit from paired commas.

Subject: A gray tabby cat asleep, curled on a folded mustard-yellow knitted blanket on a wooden sill
Focal point: the cat's sleeping face and white paws
Light: soft daylight from the window at the upper left

What it saw, back to front

  1. The blue wall
  2. The window
  3. The wooden sill
  4. The knitted blanket
  5. The sleeping cat
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint-along, back to front, is the owner's pick for beginner acrylic and the only technique with version 2 keys. It suits this picture: a flat wall and window behind, then the sill, the blanket, and the cat on top, each built dark to light.

Passed onBlock in, then build up

It has no version 2 keys (v2_step_range, v2_rules), so pipeline v2 can't plan with it; it also starts from a toned ground and a block-in the owner's paint-along skips.

How the paint recipes were worked out15 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order13 steps

Back to front: the wall and the sill first, painted straight through under everything, then the window on the wall, then the blanket, then the cat on top of it. Inside the blanket and the cat: base coat, shade, light marks; for the cat, white patches, pink, stripes, then the light fur last.

  1. 1. Blend the blue wall

    The farthest thing, and the biggest: it goes on first and runs under everything.

  2. 2. Blend the wooden sill

    The sill is the other background area; it runs under the blanket so its strokes stay long.

  3. 3. Block in the window

    The window sits on the wall, so it comes after it; one gray-blue shape first.

  4. 4. Light the window with leaves

    The leaves outside are lighter than the base and need it dry under them.

  5. 5. Light the window frame bars

    The white bars are the lightest thing in the window, so they go last there.

  6. 6. Block in the blanket's two rolls

    The blanket is in front of the sill and behind the cat; its two rolls go on as one coat.

  7. 7. Shade the blanket's folds

    The dark crease between the rolls comes before the light stitches that sit on top.

  8. 8. Light the knit stitches

    The knit stitches are the lit texture, over a dry base, so the ochre shows between.

  9. 9. Block in the cat

    The subject goes on last, over the blanket; first its whole shape in one gray.

  10. 10. Paint the pale chest, muzzle, and paws

    The white patches need the gray dry under them and two or three coats.

  11. 11. Paint the pink ears and nose

    The pink inside the ears and the nose are a small accent on the dry gray and white.

  12. 12. Paint the tabby stripes

    The stripes and eyes are the darkest marks; they curve around the finished shape.

  13. 13. Flick in the light fur

    The light flicked fur goes last, over the stripes' edges, so it softens them.

A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • The kept outline gives the cat a short piece of the window's upper crossbar (left of the ear, about 4 to 13% across, 11 to 15% down), so that bit of white bar is cut out of the window's steps and arrives with the cat's block-in. The cat had used its two fix rounds; a points_out there would be the next thing to try. The window's lower ledge and the shadow under the paws stay with the wall.
  • Drafted the furry-animal element (filed as issue 117): the research names fur only under Flicking, so fur direction, markings as a pass, and the face last are general practice.
  • The flicking card is written for grass (fan brush, upward strokes, blades); I rewrote its motion and result lines for fur. A fur note on that card, or a per-lesson card, would help.
  • Rewrote drafted lines from build-from-pieces (window bars, blanket rolls, cat body: its ( ) curved pieces don't fit rectangles), curved-strokes (its pumpkin and balloon example, on the blanket folds and the cat's white), thick-to-thin ('for branches and grass', on stripes), and liner ('for branches', a step later dropped).
  • Small features that share a paint with a bigger pass come in with that pass: the closed eyes arrive with the stripes' charcoal, the whiskers with the white. A planned eyes-and-whiskers step was left with nothing to show and was dropped; the eyes and whiskers are named in the tips of the steps that show them. A liner step for them would need its own measured paint.
  • No Agent tool was available, so the text review was done in the same context (review_context: same).
  • The wall step's picture shows a dotted blue trace along the bottom (the wall's outline taking slivers along the blanket's lower edge); the sill covers it in the next step.

Known problems

Where the pictures aren't quite right. Paint it the way the step says and use the picture as a guide.

  • Step 1, Blend the blue wall: Step 1's picture shows a dotted blue trace along the bottom where the blanket's edge will be, left by the outlines.
  • Step 9, Block in the cat: The cat's outline took a piece of the window's upper cross bar, so that bit turns gray in step 9 and white again in the last step.
  • The text review was done by the same session that wrote the text, not a fresh one.
